questions.stem: A 14 year old boy has a 2 week history of drinking large amounts of water, getting up at night to pass urine and losing 5 kg. He is tired and his school work has suffered. His BMI is 17 kg/m². Urine dipstick shows glucose 4+ and ketones 2+. His capillary glucose is 21 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A young slim patient with rapid onset of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and ketonuria has type 1 diabetes from absolute insulin deficiency.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Young + slim + **rapid** symptoms + weight loss + **ketones** = type 1.

elim: Polyuria and thirst but no glycosuria or ketones.
Usually mild, ketosis-negative, with a strong family history.
Glucose would be normal.
Gradual onset in older or obese patients; weight loss with ketones suggests absolute insulin deficiency.

steps.x: **D. Type 1 diabetes mellitus.** Type 1: young, rapid onset, weight loss, ketosis.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl with a BMI of 38 kg/m² attends her GP for tiredness. She has no weight loss. There are velvety dark plaques on the back of her neck and in both axillae. Her father has type 2 diabetes. Investigations: HbA1c 56 mmol/mol (<42), urine ketones negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Obesity with acanthosis nigricans and a diabetic HbA1c without ketosis is type 2 diabetes, increasingly seen in obese young people.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Acanthosis nigricans** = insulin resistance; obese young people now get type 2.

elim: Pigmentation is generalised with low BP and hyponatraemia.
Would give striae, proximal myopathy and hypertension; acanthosis alone points to insulin resistance.
Can cause acanthosis, but an HbA1c of 56 is diabetes.
No weight loss or ketones; acanthosis indicates insulin resistance.

steps.x: **E. Type 2 diabetes mellitus.** Type 2 increasingly affects young obese patients; acanthosis is the sign of insulin resistance.

questions.stem: A 23 year old slim man has glycosuria at a work medical. His fasting glucose is 8.1 mmol/L. His mother and his maternal grandmother were both diagnosed with 'non-insulin dependent' diabetes in their early twenties. Anti-GAD antibodies are negative and C-peptide is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely genetic defect?
questions.e: Autosomal dominant diabetes before 25 with normal C-peptide and negative antibodies is MODY; MODY 3 is due to an HNF-1 alpha defect.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely genetic defect? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Three generations + under 25 + antibody-negative = **MODY**. Commonest: MODY 3, **HNF-1α**.

elim: Linked to type 1 diabetes, which is antibody-positive with low C-peptide.
Causes severe insulin resistance syndromes, rare.
Maternal inheritance with deafness.
Associated with autoimmune type 1 diabetes.

steps.x: **B. HNF-1 alpha mutation.** MODY resembles type 2 but occurs under 25; MODY 3 = HNF-1 alpha; treat with sulfonylurea.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with hypertension has an HbA1c of 51 mmol/mol (<42) at his annual review. A year ago it was 40 mmol/mol. His weight is unchanged. His medicines are amlodipine, bendroflumethiazide (added 9 months ago) and simvastatin. He has no symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his raised HbA1c?
questions.e: Thiazide diuretics such as bendroflumethiazide are a recognised drug cause of hyperglycaemia; the rise followed starting it.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his raised HbA1c? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
New thiazide then rising HbA1c = drug-induced hyperglycaemia.

elim: Calcium channel blockers do not raise glucose.
Possible cause of diabetes but nothing else suggests it.
Consider with weight loss over 60; his weight is stable.
Statins raise risk slightly, but the new thiazide is the recognised culprit.

steps.x: **B. Bendroflumethiazide.** Bendroflumethiazide is a recognised drug cause of hyperglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought in from a care home with 4 days of confusion and reduced intake. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg; mucous membranes are dry. Investigations: glucose 46 mmol/L, blood ketones 0.8 mmol/L (<0.6), venous pH 7.36, serum osmolality 352 mOsm/kg (275–295).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Urinary tract infection without metabolic disturbance
questions.e: Very high glucose, high osmolality and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis in type 2 diabetes is HHS: residual insulin suppresses ketogenesis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Glucose very high + **osmolality** high + **no acidosis** in older type 2 = HHS.

elim: pH is normal and ketones only slightly raised.
Glucose is very high.
pH would be low.
Could precipitate it, but glucose and osmolality are grossly abnormal.

steps.x: **B. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.** Type 2 risks HHS (high glucose, dehydration); type 1 risks DKA.

questions.stem: A 20 year old student with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting and abdominal pain for 12 hours after missing insulin doses during exams. Her respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute, pulse rate 116 bpm. Investigations: glucose 24 mmol/L, blood ketones 4.8 mmol/L (<0.6), venous pH 7.15, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L (22–29).
questions.q: Which acute complication is most likely?
questions.e: Type 1 diabetes with omitted insulin, vomiting, ketones over 3 and acidosis is DKA.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which acute complication is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Type 1 + missed insulin + **ketones + acidosis** = DKA.

elim: Would not explain ketones and acidosis with high glucose.
Does not cause ketoacidosis with glucose 24.
Typically type 2 without significant ketosis or acidosis.
Glucose is high.

steps.x: **B. Diabetic ketoacidosis.** DKA risk in type 1: never stop insulin.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 18 years says his feet feel as though he is walking on cotton wool. He has tripped twice in the dark. Examination shows reduced pinprick and vibration sense to above both ankles, absent ankle reflexes and a positive Romberg test. His hands are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding as his condition progresses?
o: Asymmetrical proximal weakness of one thigh
Loss of sensation in a single dermatome
Sensory loss spreading to the hands in a glove distribution
Upper motor neurone signs in the legs
questions.e: Diabetic neuropathy is a length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy: it starts in the legs and, when it reaches mid-calf, the hands become involved (glove-and-stocking).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding as his condition progresses? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Longest nerves affected first: feet, then hands = **glove and stocking**.

elim: That is diabetic amyotrophy, not the typical polyneuropathy.
Not a length-dependent pattern.
Radiculopathy, not polyneuropathy.
Peripheral neuropathy gives lower motor neurone signs.

steps.x: **D. Sensory loss spreading to the hands in a glove distribution.** Diabetic neuropathy: length-dependent, glove-and-stocking, starts in the legs.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a deep ulcer on the sole of her right foot with green discharge and a sweet, grape-like smell. The foot is cold with absent pedal pulses. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm. Probe-to-bone test is positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Green discharge with a sweet smell suggests Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common organism in diabetic foot ulcers; with ischaemia this is limb-threatening and needs urgent secondary care.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Green** + **grape smell** = Pseudomonas.

elim: Causes gas gangrene with crepitus.
A urinary pathogen; does not give green discharge.
Causes spreading cellulitis without green discharge.
Fungal; does not cause this deep ulcer.

steps.x: **D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa.** Diabetic foot ulcer with ischaemia: limb-threatening; Pseudomonas common.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with type 1 diabetes for 30 years has 6 months of early satiety and bloating. He sometimes vomits food he ate the previous evening. His glucose readings swing unpredictably with frequent post-meal hypoglycaemia. Upper GI endoscopy is normal. He has retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
o: Gastric outlet obstruction from peptic ulcer
questions.e: Long-standing diabetes with other microvascular complications, early satiety, bloating and vomiting undigested food suggests gastroparesis from impaired vagal motility.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: vomits food he ate the previous evening
steps.x: Vomiting old food + normal scope + autonomic damage = **gastroparesis**.

elim: Endoscopy is normal.
Heartburn, not vomiting of food from the day before.
Gives diarrhoea and weight loss rather than vomiting undigested food.
Causes constipation and weight gain, not this picture.

steps.x: **B. Diabetic gastroparesis.** Gastroparesis: reduced vagal/ACh motility, delayed gastric emptying.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with type 1 diabetes diagnosed 2 years ago has 3 months of palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss despite a good appetite and a fine tremor. Her HbA1c has risen from 52 to 64 mmol/mol. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and regular.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to be abnormal?
questions.e: Type 1 diabetes is associated with other autoimmune conditions, notably thyroid disease (here hyperthyroidism), hence routine thyroid function tests.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which investigation is most likely to be abnormal? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Type 1 + hyperthyroid features = associated **autoimmune thyroid** disease.

elim: Coeliac would give diarrhoea, not tremor and heat intolerance.
Addison's gives weight loss with fatigue and hypotension, not tremor.
No abdominal pain.
Phaeochromocytoma is rare; autoimmune thyroid disease is far likelier.

steps.x: **D. Thyroid function tests.** Check TFTs in type 1 diabetes: autoimmune clustering.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension and a cholesterol of 6.4 mmol/L smokes 10 cigarettes a day. He asks which complication is the commonest cause of death in people with diabetes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely answer?
questions.e: Macrovascular disease (cardiovascular disease) from accelerated atherosclerosis driven by hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia and hypertension is the main killer.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely answer? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Diabetes + BP + lipids + smoking = **macrovascular** atherosclerosis.

elim: An acute complication, mainly type 1, and uncommon as a cause of death.
Important, but cardiovascular disease kills more.
Causes blindness, not death.
Rarely fatal compared with cardiovascular disease.

steps.x: **A. Cardiovascular disease.** Chronic complications: microvascular (eyes, nerves, kidneys) and macrovascular (CVD).

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman with a BMI of 34 kg/m² has a raised HbA1c on a routine check. Her fasting insulin level is high and her C-peptide is raised. She has no weight loss or ketones.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hyperglycaemia?
o: Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency
questions.e: High insulin and C-peptide with obesity show type 2 diabetes: peripheral insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell dysfunction causing relative deficiency.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hyperglycaemia? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Plenty of insulin but still high glucose = **resistance**.

elim: Type 1; insulin and C-peptide would be low.
Type 1; C-peptide would be low.
Rare; gives necrolytic migratory erythema.
Acromegaly has characteristic features absent here.

steps.x: **E. Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency.** Type 2: insulin resistance + relative deficiency.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has 2 months of thirst, passing urine frequently, tiredness and blurred vision. He has lost 3 kg. His BMI is 31 kg/m². A random venous plasma glucose is 15.2 mmol/L. Urine ketones are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Symptomatic hyperglycaemia with a random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L confirms diabetes; obesity, gradual onset and no ketones make it type 2.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Symptoms + random glucose **≥11.1** = diabetes; obese, ketone-negative = type 2.

elim: Glucose would be normal.
Causes thirst and polyuria but glucose would be normal.
Random glucose of 15.2 with symptoms is diabetes, not prediabetes.
Ketone-negative, gradual and obese favours type 2.

steps.x: **E. Type 2 diabetes mellitus.** Classic symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man of Nigerian heritage has a routine HbA1c of 45 mmol/mol (<42). He has no symptoms. His BMI is 29 kg/m². He has sickle cell trait.

visual.title: HbA1c
visual.caption: 42–47 is prediabetes; 48 or more is diabetes.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?
o: Prediabetes; HbA1c may be unreliable, so check fasting glucose
questions.e: An HbA1c of 42–47 mmol/mol is prediabetes, but HbA1c is less reliable in sickle cell trait, so glucose-based testing helps.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate interpretation and next step? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
42–47 = **prediabetes**; haemoglobin variant = HbA1c unreliable.

elim: 45 is below the diagnostic 48.
42–47 is prediabetes.
Haemoglobin variants make HbA1c less reliable; use glucose.
No features of type 1.

steps.x: **C. Prediabetes; HbA1c may be unreliable, so check fasting glucose.** HbA1c 42–47 = prediabetes; less reliable in sickle cell trait.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has an HbA1c of 49 mmol/mol (<42) at an NHS health check. She feels well and has no thirst or polyuria. Her BMI is 30 kg/m². She asks if she has diabetes. Her full blood count and renal function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Diagnose type 2 diabetes and start treatment
Oral glucose tolerance test only if symptomatic
questions.e: HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol is diagnostic of type 2 diabetes, but if asymptomatic a second abnormal reading is needed to confirm.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Above 48 but **asymptomatic** = needs a **second** reading.

elim: Asymptomatic people need a second abnormal result.
Not the standard confirmation.
49 is in the diabetic range, not 42–47.
No weight loss or age over 60 with red flags.

steps.x: **D. Repeat HbA1c to confirm.** Diagnosis: HbA1c ≥48; asymptomatic needs confirmation.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl is brought to the GP with 10 days of bedwetting, thirst and weight loss. She is alert and drinking well. Her mother has hypothyroidism. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: In suspected type 1 diabetes the first-line test is a random plasma glucose (same-day referral if high); HbA1c is first-line for suspected type 2.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Child + rapid symptoms = suspected **type 1** = **random glucose**.

elim: First-line for suspected type 2; lags behind rapid-onset type 1.
Delays diagnosis in suspected type 1.
Second-line to confirm the type, not to diagnose diabetes.
Not diagnostic.

steps.x: **E. Random plasma glucose.** Suspected type 1: random plasma glucose. Suspected type 2: HbA1c.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man was labelled as having type 2 diabetes a year ago. He is slim, and despite metformin his HbA1c has risen from 58 to 84 mmol/mol and he has lost 6 kg. He had ketones 1.8 mmol/L at a recent appointment.

visual.title: HbA1c on metformin
visual.caption: Rising HbA1c despite metformin in a slim, ketotic man suggests type 1.

questions.q: Which investigation would best determine his type of diabetes?
questions.e: Low C-peptide and positive anti-GAD antibodies distinguish type 1 (autoimmune) from other types; this slim, ketotic patient may have late-onset autoimmune diabetes.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which investigation would best determine his type of diabetes? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Slim + failing metformin + ketones = possible **autoimmune** diabetes.

elim: Does not distinguish types.
Monitors control; does not classify.
MODY is ketosis-negative with a strong family history.
Diagnoses diabetes, not its type.

steps.x: **A. C-peptide and anti-GAD antibodies.** C-peptide (low) and anti-GAD (positive) confirm type 1.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has new-onset diabetes with an HbA1c of 70 mmol/mol (<42). He has lost 8 kg in 2 months without trying and has a dull ache in his upper abdomen. His BMI is 22 kg/m². His bilirubin is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Over 60 with new-onset diabetes and weight loss, an urgent CT abdomen is considered to exclude pancreatic cancer.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Over 60 + new diabetes + **weight loss** = think **pancreatic cancer**.

elim: Autoimmune diabetes is unlikely at 71 with these red flags.
Symptoms do not point to the colon.
Delays investigation of possible cancer.
Not relevant.

steps.x: **E. Urgent CT abdomen.** New diabetes with weight loss over 60: urgent CT abdomen.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has type 2 diabetes for 6 years. At her annual review her BP is 142/84 mmHg and eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m². She asks which test is used to screen her kidneys for diabetic damage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Diabetic nephropathy is screened with urine ACR; retinopathy with retinal screening and neuropathy with foot examination.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Early diabetic kidney damage = albuminuria = **ACR**.

elim: Not a screening test.
Does not detect early nephropathy.
Not a nephropathy screen.
Not sensitive enough for early albuminuria.

steps.x: **D. Urine albumin:creatinine ratio.** Complication screening: ACR (kidney), retinal screening (eye), foot examination (nerves).

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus insulin is reviewed in clinic. He feels shaky and sweaty mid-morning several times a week. He checks his glucose only once a day before bed. His HbA1c was last checked 14 months ago.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate monitoring plan?
o: Capillary glucose at least 4 times a day and HbA1c every 3–6 months
questions.e: In type 1 diabetes, capillary glucose is checked at least 4 times a day (before meals and bed), useful in suspected hypoglycaemia, and HbA1c every 3–6 months.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate monitoring plan? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Possible hypos + poor monitoring = **CBG ≥4/day** and **HbA1c 3–6 monthly**.

elim: Far too infrequent for type 1.
Does not monitor glycaemia.
Should be every 3–6 months.
Does not detect hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: **A. Capillary glucose at least 4 times a day and HbA1c every 3–6 months.** Type 1 monitoring: CBG ≥4 times a day, HbA1c every 3–6 months.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with type 1 diabetes, weighing 60 kg, is admitted for elective surgery and is eating normally. The team calculates a total daily insulin dose of 40 units for a basal-bolus regimen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate split of her insulin?
o: 10 units rapid-acting with meals and 30 units long-acting
20 units rapid-acting with meals and 20 units long-acting
24 units rapid-acting with meals and 16 units long-acting
questions.e: Basal-bolus insulin in hospital is split roughly 3/5 short-acting with meals and 2/5 long-acting basal: 24 and 16 units.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate split of her insulin? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: total daily insulin dose of 40 units
steps.x: 3/5 of 40 = **24** with meals; 2/5 = **16** basal.

elim: Too much basal; meal insulin should be the larger share.
Equal split; the notes give roughly 3/5 to 2/5.
Type 1 needs meal-time bolus insulin.
Without basal insulin she is at risk of DKA.

steps.x: **C. 24 units rapid-acting with meals and 16 units long-acting.** Type 1: lifelong basal-bolus, roughly 3/5 bolus and 2/5 basal.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man with type 1 diabetes on insulin detemir and insulin aspart asks what glucose targets he should aim for. His BMI is 23 kg/m². His HbA1c is 61 mmol/mol (<42).
questions.q: Which are the most appropriate targets?
o: 4–10 mmol/L at all times, HbA1c 75 mmol/mol
5–7 mmol/L on waking, 4–7 mmol/L before meals, HbA1c 48 mmol/mol
Below 4 mmol/L before meals, HbA1c 40 mmol/mol
Under 11 mmol/L before meals, HbA1c 53 mmol/mol
questions.e: Type 1 targets are 5–7 mmol/L on waking, 4–7 mmol/L before meals and HbA1c 48 mmol/mol; CGM and pumps can help meet them.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which are the most appropriate targets? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Type 1 targets: **5–7** waking, **4–7** before meals, HbA1c **48**.

elim: Too lax for type 1.
Targets are too high.
Below 4 is hypoglycaemia.
Above the type 1 targets.

steps.x: **B. 5–7 mmol/L on waking, 4–7 mmol/L before meals, HbA1c 48 mmol/mol.** Type 1: targets 5–7 waking, 4–7 pre-meal, HbA1c 48.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with type 2 diabetes takes modified-release metformin and dapagliflozin. After 6 months his HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol (<42). His BMI is 31 kg/m², eGFR 74 mL/min/1.73m². He has no cardiovascular disease, heart failure or kidney disease.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue current treatment and recheck in 12 months
questions.e: With no comorbidities, the standard next step after dual therapy is a DPP-4 inhibitor such as sitagliptin, which is weight-neutral and useful in obesity.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no cardiovascular disease, heart failure or kidney disease
steps.x: Uncomplicated, HbA1c >58 on dual therapy = add **DPP-4 inhibitor**.

elim: Metformin should continue; pioglitazone causes weight gain and fractures.
Insulin is for when multiple oral agents fail.
HbA1c above 58 needs intensifying.
Removes a protective agent and risks hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: **B. Add sitagliptin.** Standard second step: DPP-4 inhibitor (sitagliptin); rarely pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. She has chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. She previously had severe lactic acidosis on metformin and is advised never to take it again. Her eGFR is 55 mL/min/1.73m². Her HbA1c is 59 mmol/mol (<42).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: When metformin is contraindicated and there is established CVD or chronic heart failure, SGLT-2 inhibitor monotherapy (e.g. dapagliflozin) is used.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Metformin contraindicated + **heart failure** = **SGLT2 monotherapy**.

elim: Risks hypoglycaemia and offers no heart failure benefit.
Not first-line.
Contraindicated in heart failure.
Neutral; an SGLT2 inhibitor is preferred with heart failure.

steps.x: **A. Dapagliflozin.** Metformin CI with CVD/HF: SGLT2 inhibitor alone; avoid pioglitazone in HF.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with type 2 diabetes takes metformin, dapagliflozin and gliclazide. He has had two falls this month after feeling sweaty and confused before lunch. His HbA1c is 46 mmol/mol (<42). He lives alone.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his falls?
questions.e: Sulfonylureas such as gliclazide cause hypoglycaemia; his HbA1c is below the 53 target for those on hypoglycaemia-causing drugs, so the dose should be reduced.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his falls? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Pre-meal sweating/confusion on a **sulfonylurea** = hypoglycaemia.

elim: Possible, but sweating and confusion before meals point to hypoglycaemia.
Not in a type 2 patient with low-normal glucose.
Gives acidosis with illness, not episodic pre-meal symptoms.
He is not on pioglitazone.

steps.x: **C. Gliclazide-induced hypoglycaemia.** Gliclazide causes hypos; target HbA1c 53 on hypoglycaemia-causing drugs.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Her BMI is 40 kg/m². She has no cardiovascular disease and eGFR is 96 mL/min/1.73m². She has started modified-release metformin and dapagliflozin. Her HbA1c is 69 mmol/mol (<42).
questions.q: Which additional drug is most appropriate?
questions.e: Early-onset type 2 (under 40) or a BMI ≥37 kg/m² warrants adding a GLP-1 agonist such as semaglutide (no weight gain) to the two core drugs.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which additional drug is most appropriate? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Young (<40) + BMI ≥37 = add a **GLP-1 agonist**.

elim: Causes weight gain and hypoglycaemia.
Causes weight gain; reserved for failure of other agents.
A weight-loss drug, not a diabetes agent here.
Causes weight gain and fractures.

steps.x: **E. Semaglutide.** Early-onset or obese type 2: add semaglutide (or tirzepatide).

questions.stem: A 54 year old man of Black African family origin with type 2 diabetes has clinic BP readings of 152/94 and 148/92 mmHg, confirmed on ambulatory monitoring. His ACR is 2 mg/mmol and eGFR 85 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antihypertensive?
questions.e: In diabetes, hypertension is treated with an ACE inhibitor or ARB; an ARB such as losartan is preferred in Black patients.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate antihypertensive? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Diabetes + hypertension = ACEi/ARB; Black = **ARB** (losartan).

elim: First-line for Black patients without diabetes; with diabetes an ACEi/ARB is used.
Raises glucose; not first-line.
Not first-line for hypertension.
A late add-on.

steps.x: **E. Losartan.** Diabetic hypertension: ACEi or ARB, ARB preferred in Black patients.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has burning, shooting pain in both feet for 4 months, worst at night. She has reduced pinprick sensation to the ankles. She has no history of heart disease, glaucoma or urinary retention. Paracetamol has not helped.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: First-line treatment for painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy is a tricyclic antidepressant such as amitriptyline; alternatives are pregabalin, duloxetine or gabapentin.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: reduced pinprick sensation to the ankles
steps.x: Painful neuropathy with no TCA contraindication = **amitriptyline**.

elim: Opioids are not first-line for neuropathic pain.
Not effective for neuropathic pain.
No role.
Reserved for localised pain when oral options are unsuitable.

steps.x: **A. Amitriptyline.** Painful diabetic neuropathy: amitriptyline; alternatives pregabalin, duloxetine, gabapentin.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with type 2 diabetes on modified-release metformin has profuse diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days after a family meal. He can sip water only. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. His capillary glucose is 11 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about his metformin?
o: Continue metformin at the same dose
Suspend metformin until he is eating and drinking normally
questions.e: Metformin increases lactic acidosis risk with dehydration, so it is suspended during intercurrent illness with diarrhoea or vomiting (sick day rules).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate advice about his metformin? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Dehydrating illness on metformin = **pause it** (lactic acidosis).

elim: Risks lactic acidosis with dehydration.
Increases lactic acidosis risk.
Only a temporary suspension is needed.
Not needed; risk of hypoglycaemia when not eating.

steps.x: **D. Suspend metformin until he is eating and drinking normally.** Sick day rules: suspend metformin in D&V; never stop insulin.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with type 2 diabetes is an inpatient recovering from pneumonia. He is eating and drinking. His capillary glucose this afternoon is 16.4 mmol/L with no ketones. He is alert, pulse rate 84 bpm. He is on metformin and his usual dose was given.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 1 hour
questions.e: Hyperglycaemia in hospital without DKA or HHS is treated with a correction dose of 2–6 units of short or rapid-acting subcutaneous insulin.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate immediate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Simple inpatient hyperglycaemia, no ketones = small **subcutaneous correction** dose.

elim: He is not dehydrated or in HHS.
Would worsen hyperglycaemia.
That is the DKA regimen.
Not indicated.

steps.x: **A. 2–6 units of subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin.** Inpatient hyperglycaemia: 2–6 units SC rapid-acting insulin.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. She has chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 17 mL/min/1.73m². She has no heart failure. Her HbA1c is 60 mmol/mol (<42) and BMI 27 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: A new type 2 diagnosis with eGFR below 20 is started on a DPP-4 inhibitor (e.g. linagliptin); at eGFR 20–30 an SGLT2 inhibitor plus a DPP-4 inhibitor is used.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
eGFR **<20** = **DPP-4 inhibitor** alone.

elim: SGLT2 inhibitors are started with eGFR of 20 or more.
High hypoglycaemia risk in advanced CKD.
Contraindicated at eGFR below 30.
Fluid retention, fractures; not first choice.

steps.x: **C. Linagliptin.** CKD: eGFR <20 DPP-4; eGFR 20–30 SGLT2 + DPP-4.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin has a urine ACR of 48 mg/mmol (<3) on two samples and eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73m². He has had a myocardial infarction. His HbA1c is 51 mmol/mol (<42) and BP 128/78 mmHg on ramipril.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition?
questions.e: SGLT2 inhibitors are indicated with diabetic nephropathy (ACR ≥35 mg/mmol) plus high CVD risk, giving renal and cardiovascular protection independent of glucose lowering.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate addition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
ACR **≥35** + CVD = SGLT2 for **organ protection**, even with good HbA1c.

elim: Adds hypoglycaemia risk without renal or cardiac protection.
HbA1c is near target; no organ protection.
Fluid retention; no renal protection.
No organ protection.

steps.x: **A. Empagliflozin.** SGLT2 inhibitors: diabetic nephropathy (ACR ≥35), heart failure, ASCVD.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 40 years and autonomic neuropathy feels lightheaded on standing, especially in the morning. Her BP is 138/80 mmHg lying and 104/66 mmHg standing. She takes no antihypertensives. ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Diabetes-related postural hypotension from autonomic neuropathy is managed first by increasing dietary sodium chloride.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Autonomic postural drop = expand volume with **salt**.

elim: A diuretic would worsen postural drop.
Lowers BP further.
Never stop insulin in type 1.
An alpha-blocker worsens postural hypotension.

steps.x: **B. Increase dietary sodium chloride.** Diabetic postural hypotension: increase dietary salt.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. His C-peptide is undetectable and islet autoantibodies are positive. His parents ask what has happened to his pancreas.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Autoantibody blockade of the insulin receptor
T-cell mediated destruction of islet beta cells
questions.e: Type 1 diabetes is T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic islet beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
No C-peptide + autoantibodies = beta cells destroyed by **T cells**.

elim: Seen in type 2 diabetes.
A rare cause of insulin resistance.
Pancreatic diabetes from chronic pancreatitis or CF.
Type 2 mechanism.

steps.x: **E. T-cell mediated destruction of islet beta cells.** Type 1: T-cell mediated beta-cell destruction.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes for 15 years has retinopathy, microalbuminuria and a glove-and-stocking sensory neuropathy. Her HbA1c has been above 80 mmol/mol for a decade.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism linking her complications?
o: Autoimmune attack on nerves and vessels
questions.e: Chronic hyperglycaemia causes non-enzymatic glycation forming AGEs, which damage endothelium, nerves and basement membrane, underlying retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism linking her complications? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Years of high glucose sugar-coat proteins = **AGEs**.

elim: Not the mechanism of chronic diabetic damage.
Acute metabolic change, not chronic tissue damage.
Her glucose is persistently high.
Metformin can cause it but does not explain retinopathy and nephropathy.

steps.x: **C. Formation of advanced glycation end-products.** Microvascular damage: AGEs damage endothelium, nerves and basement membrane.

questions.stem: A medical student compares two patients: a 19 year old with type 1 diabetes who has ketones 5.2 mmol/L and pH 7.1, and an 80 year old with type 2 diabetes who has glucose 52 mmol/L, ketones 0.5 mmol/L and normal pH.
questions.q: Which best explains why the first patient developed ketoacidosis?
o: Absolute insulin deficiency allows unrestrained ketogenesis
questions.e: In DKA absolute insulin deficiency allows unrestrained lipolysis and ketogenesis; in HHS residual insulin suppresses ketogenesis but not hyperglycaemia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best explains why the first patient developed ketoacidosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Even a little insulin stops ketones. **None** = ketoacidosis.

elim: Diet does not drive DKA.
The second patient has higher glucose without ketosis.
Ketones are excreted; the problem is overproduction.
Age is not the mechanism; residual insulin is.

steps.x: **A. Absolute insulin deficiency allows unrestrained ketogenesis.** DKA: absolute deficiency. HHS: residual insulin blocks ketogenesis.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with type 2 diabetes is started on dapagliflozin. Four weeks later he has his first episode of genital thrush and his urine dipstick shows glucose 4+, although his capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his glycosuria?
o: Inhibition of glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule
questions.e: SGLT2 inhibitors block glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule, causing glycosuria (and genital thrush) even at normal glucose.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his glycosuria? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Glucose in urine at normal blood glucose = **blocked proximal reabsorption**.

elim: GFR change is not the main effect.
That is how sulfonylureas work.
That is furosemide.
That is metformin.

steps.x: **C. Inhibition of glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule.** SGLT2 inhibitors: proximal tubule glycosuria.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes has nausea, early satiety and vomiting of undigested food. A gastric emptying study shows 70% retention at 4 hours (<10%). Her other autonomic features include postural dizziness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her symptoms?
questions.e: Diabetic gastroparesis results from impaired vagal tone and reduced acetylcholine-mediated motility, delaying gastric emptying.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her symptoms? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Autonomic neuropathy + delayed emptying = loss of **vagal** drive.

elim: Mechanical, would show on endoscopy.
Causes dyspepsia, not delayed emptying of this degree.
Zollinger-Ellison causes ulcers and diarrhoea.
Causes bloating and diarrhoea, not delayed gastric emptying.

steps.x: **D. Reduced vagal acetylcholine-mediated gastric motility.** Gastroparesis: impaired vagal tone, reduced ACh motility.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man with type 1 diabetes for 25 years has ankle swelling. He has background retinopathy and reduced vibration sense in both feet. His BP is 146/90 mmHg. Investigations: urine ACR 92 mg/mmol (<3), eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m², urine microscopy shows no red cell casts.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his proteinuria?
questions.e: Long-standing diabetes with other microvascular complications (retinopathy, neuropathy) and rising albuminuria is diabetic nephropathy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his proteinuria? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Retinopathy + neuropathy + albuminuria = the **microvascular triad**.

elim: Presents with visible haematuria after infection.
A childhood nephrotic syndrome with normal renal function.
Nephritic with haematuria and red cell casts after a sore throat.
Gives hypertension and a bland urine without heavy albuminuria.

steps.x: **A. Diabetic nephropathy.** Microvascular complications: retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy; screen with ACR.
